title: Supreme Court of Maryland restores Bereano’s law license, 26 years later
summary: The Supreme Court of Maryland restored the law license Friday of Annapolis power lobbyist Bruce Bereano, more than 26 years after it disbarred him in the wake of a federal mail fraud conviction linked to his lobbying firm.
content:
by Steve Crane, Maryland Matters March 21, 2026

by Steve Crane, Maryland Matters March 21, 2026

The Supreme Court of Maryland restored the law license Friday of Annapolis power lobbyist Bruce Bereano, more than 26 years after it disbarred him in the wake of a federal mail fraud conviction linked to his lobbying firm.

In a one-page order, the court said it was granting the petition for reinstatement from “Bruce Charles Bereano … as a member of the Bar of Maryland.”

Bereano said he was “deeply appreciative” of the ruling, and that he cried in happiness on receiving an email from the court Friday morning notifying him of it.

“For the first time in 25 years, I feel emotionally whole again,” said Bereano, who said he always “loved practicing law.”

It’s not as though he needed his law license to get by: For decades, Bereano has routinely been cited as one of the top lobbyists in Annapolis, in the years before and after his conviction. Bereano reported 49 clients in his last report with the Maryland State Ethics Commission, from the Anne Arundel County Fair and Earleigh Heights Volunteer Fire Co. to Washington Gas and the state’s medical society.

Bereano lost his law license in January 2000, after several years of appeals played out in his November 1994 conviction in federal court on seven counts of mail fraud in connection with campaign contributions funneled through his lobbying firm. Prosecutors said the scheme was funded with invoices fraudulently billed to his lobbying clients.

Court records show there were several ways Bereano was able get money to campaigns without revealing the sources of the donations. He asked his employees to make campaign contributions in their own names, and then he reimbursed them for the cost of the donations with a check drawn on the firm’s account.

He also had his workers cash company checks made out to them, then return the cash to him. Bereano would then dole that money out to family members, who handed it back to his political action committee.

The checks involved in the scheme were often recorded as items like “legislative entertainment,” and billed to lobbying clients, even though no such service was performed. He was originally convicted of diverting $16,000 in clients’ funds that way, but a later ruling said prosecutors had only shown $600 in such improper payments. Still, that money was fraudulently billed to clients who did not know they were making campaign donations, courts said.

Bereano applied to have his law license restored in 2019, but the petition went nowhere. He said Friday that he thinks his most recent petition was filed a year or so ago.

Bereano said he has accepted his convictions and has not challenged them since his appeals were exhausted. That will not change with the restoration of his law license, he said.

“I don’t dwell on it,” Bereano said. “You learn from all the different experiences in life, and that’s what this was.”

Although he doesn’t know who would hire him as a lawyer, Bereano said he would “very much like to be back in a courtroom,” In the meantime, it’s enough to have the license back, “because I wanted to feel whole again. I was very proud to be a lawyer.”
